newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM wants hated Pol Pot captured alive.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM wants hated Pol Pot captured alive.

text.p: Cambodia's first prime minister said on Tuesday he wanted Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot captured alive and brought before an international tribunal for the crimes of his "killing fields" regime.
"I hope that we will be able to take Pol Pot alive and send him to an international court," First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters at a school graduation ceremony in Phnom Penh.
Pol Pot, mastermind of the 1975-79 government, is reported to be on the run in the north of the country after most of his fighters deserted him.

There was no new information on Pol Pot's whereabouts, Ranariddh said. A senior military official was scheduled to go into the northern Khmer Rouge stronghold of Anlong Veng on Wednesday to learn more about the situation, he added.
"I would not say for the time being if Pol Pot would be able to be captured or passed away or killed, I do not know," Ranariddh said.

He also had no further updates on Briton Christopher Howes, who was kidnapped in March 1996. Ranariddh said earlier that Howes was believed to be with Pol Pot's group along with several senior Khmer Rouge officials, including the president of the rebels' provisional government, Khieu Samphan, who he said were taken as hostages.
In an apparent response to comments on Monday by his co-premier, Hun Sen, Ranariddh said there was nothing wrong with talking to the rebels in Anlong Veng.
He said Hun Sen had made deals with other rebels. Hun Sen helped obtain a royal pardon for former Khmer Rouge foreign minister Ieng Sary last year.

Ranariddh revealed on Monday he had held a secret meeting three weeks ago with Khieu Samphan, prompting Hun Sen to call all talks with remaining hardliners illegal and threatening arrest for those who negotiated with the Maoist guerrillas.
On Tuesday, Ranariddh said he would draw the line only at co-operation with Pol Pot or his northern commander, Ta Mok.
"There are only two -- Ta Mok and Pol Pot -- who will not be given any amnesty," Ranariddh said.
Ta Mok has broken with Pol Pot and disappeared, Ranariddh said.
Not everyone is convinced that Ta Mok or other rebels have broken with Pol Pot, and many question Ranariddh's statements that Khieu Samphan is now a hostage of the rebel strongman.
Analysts said the story may have been cooked up to differentiate Khieu Samphan, who wants to join a political alliance with Ranariddh, from the much-reviled Pol Pot.
About 95 percent of the Khmer Rouge fighters remaining in Anlong Veng and a group of rebels with Pol Pot want to join the government, Ranariddh has said.
The rebels, decimated by thousands of defections since last August, are split over whether to make peace.
The group reneged on a 1991 pact meant to end Cambodia's long history of conflict and have been fighting the coalition government formed after a U.N.-sponsored poll in 1993.
More than one million Cambodians died through executions, starvation, disease and hard labour during the Khmer Rouge's disastrous experiment in total communism.
